definition: Charles Babbage’s brass mechanical calculating machine design, for which Ada Lovelace wrote the world’s first computer algorithm in 1843.
Cramped brick Victorian working-class terraces built sharing three walls with neighbours, with no back garden and a shared courtyard tap.
Official paid public holidays created by Parliament in 1871 so bank clerks and factory families could enjoy seaside train trips.
A wheeled wooden changing hut pulled into the sea by a horse so modest Victorian bathers could step straight into the waves.
A local red-brick primary school built with high windows after Forster’s 1870 Education Act so every district had school places.
Global territories ruled by Britain across Canada, India, Australia, the Caribbean, and Africa—covering a quarter of Earth’s people by 1897.
Neat, looping Victorian cursive handwriting practised by older schoolchildren using sharp steel-nibbed dip pens and desk inkwells.
Proud Victorian nickname for smoky Manchester and surrounding Lancashire mill towns that spun and wove cotton cloth for the world.
Joseph Paxton’s giant iron-and-glass hall built in London’s Hyde Park for the 1851 Great Exhibition, visited by six million people.
A miner’s oil lamp enclosed inside fine wire mesh, invented by Sir Humphry Davy so underground coal gas would not explode.
Grand national and worldwide celebrations held in June 1897 to mark Queen Victoria completing sixty years on the British throne.
A tall pointed paper cone placed on a struggling pupil’s head in strict Victorian classrooms as an unfair shaming punishment.
Victorian invention sending coded electric pulses instantly along wires beside railway tracks and under oceans to spell out messages.
A cheap day-return steam train carrying working families to seaside piers like Blackpool, Brighton, and Margate on Bank Holidays.
A paid government official introduced by the 1833 Factory Act with legal power to enter textile mills and stop illegal child shifts.
Thin, watery oatmeal porridge boiled in huge copper pots and served to hungry inmates inside harsh Victorian Union Workhouses.
A Victorian child or teenager in a coal mine who wore a leather belt and chain to haul heavy wooden coal tubs along low tunnels.
An electric glass lightbulb demonstrated in Newcastle by Sir Joseph Swan in 1878, glowing brightly when current heated a carbon thread.
A coal-burning steam engine on iron wheels—like Stephenson’s Rocket or Brunel’s expresses—that pulled trains across Britain.
Landmark reform championed by Lord Shaftesbury banning all women, girls, and boys under the age of ten from working underground in pits.
Stiff, tar-soaked old ship rope that Victorian workhouse inmates and prisoners had to pick apart strand by strand with sore fingers.
The world’s first sticky postage stamp, launched in May 1840 with young Queen Victoria’s profile to carry letters anywhere in Britain for 1d.
A tall 1870s bicycle with a giant front wheel and tiny back wheel—named after Britain’s largest and smallest copper coins.
A nimble child in a Victorian cotton mill who leaned over moving spinning frames to twist snapped threads back together.
A free charity school championed by Lord Shaftesbury and Dr Barnardo teaching reading, trades, and hot meals to shoeless poor children.
Standard London Greenwich clock time adopted across British railway stations in the 1840s so train timetables matched nationwide.
Often the youngest cotton-mill child, forced to crawl right beneath clattering iron machinery to sweep up loose cotton fluff.
A young child—often aged seven or eight—sitting alone in pitch-black coal-mine tunnels to pull ventilation doors open for coal tubs.
